bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
The source prepares two particles of spin ½ in a {{trạng thái singlet|singlet state}}. Each station records +1 or −1 on its chosen axis. Two matched detections form one pair. A high click represents equal signs and a low click opposite signs.

$$A,B\in\{-1,+1\}$$

+++ A closer look
The signs are the measured components in units of ħ/2. The simulation measures spins of matter particles, so the angle in the formula is the angle between spin axes. The stations must retain emission indices or timestamps to match the signs across the two records. Shuffle one list before comparing them and the local fractions remain unchanged, but the pairing correlations disappear.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Align the axes|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Wait for several pairs to reach the detectors. Each side can give either sign, but the left result predicts the right result with certainty along the same axis. The singlet has zero total spin.

$$E(a,a)=\langle AB\rangle=-1$$

+++ A closer look
Reversing one axis reverses that station’s sign convention, so the two recorded signs always agree. Two envelopes containing opposite signs could reproduce the results for this one setting. A single pair of axes is therefore insufficient to test what is distinctive about the quantum prediction. A Bell test requires a common explanation to cover several different pairs of settings.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Reverse one axis|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Equal signs contribute +1 and opposite signs −1. Sum the products and divide by the pair count to estimate E. A change of angle clears the old counts.

$$E=P_{\rm same}-P_{\rm opp}=-\cos(a-b)$$

+++ A closer look
Perpendicular axes make equal and opposite signs equally likely. A short run can favor one by chance. Make two columns of matched results and a third containing their products. The mean of the third column differs from the product of the first two means. Each local mean can be close to zero while the mean product lies close to minus one.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Use perpendicular axes|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag an axis until the magnitude of E is below 0.018.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The P(A+) and P(B+) counters accumulate separately. For either counter alone, half the results are expected to be plus regardless of the distant axis.

$$P(A=+1)=P(B=+1)=\tfrac12$$

+++ A closer look
Either local sign is random, yet the two signs can almost always agree. These describe different distributions. Before turning Bob's knob, predict whether Alice's plus fraction will follow it. The count may jump up or down because a new run begins with a tiny sample. Allow more pairs to arrive, then compare the local probabilities again.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Reset the axes|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag an axis until E exceeds 0.995.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Alice chooses a or a′ and Bob chooses b or b′. For each combination average the product of the two outcomes. The CHSH combination requires all four averages.

$$S=E(a,b)+E(a,b')+E(a',b)-E(a',b')$$

+++ A closer look
The prediction row uses a = 0°, a′ = 90° and b′ = −b. Changing Bob’s angle changes both b and b′ in this calculation. One measured pair cannot be assigned to all four groups as though it had undergone four measurements. Each actual pair meets one setting combination. Independent groups for the four combinations must be built from pairs prepared in the same way at the source.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Run the four settings|thu]] For every pair, each station picks one of its two axes at random; the logbook shows the axis of each row and the graph shows four red dots.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: Why is the local bound two?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Suppose each particle carries an answer ±1 for each local axis, independent of the remote setting. On every trial one bracket below vanishes and the other is ±2.

$$A(B+B')+A'(B-B')=\pm2$$

The model is now running exactly such a source. Each pair carries a direction λ, drawn as the pair's colour. Alice records +1 when λ is within 90° of her axis, Bob records the opposite rule with his axis. The correlation becomes the pink zigzag line, and the counted |S| approaches 2 but does not exceed it.

+++ A closer look
Averaging over the same hidden-variable distribution gives |S| ≤ 2. The setting choices must be independent of the source’s hidden variables. Check the brackets first with equal B and B′ and then with opposite signs. An average of the results cannot leave the interval from minus two to plus two. Stochastic local responses are included by incorporating local randomness into the hidden variables.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Switch to the quantum singlet source|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Set b halfway between Alice’s axes. Opposite-signed correlations combine with the minus sign on the last term, pushing the magnitude above the local bound.

$$|S(45^\circ)|=2\sqrt{2}$$

+++ A closer look
For the axes shown in the |S| row, S is −2(cos b + sin b). Counts for the pair of settings on display supply only one term. Move b to zero so Bob's settings coincide. The terms involving a′ cancel, leaving twice the aligned-axis correlation, whose magnitude reaches the local bound. Vary b gradually to see why different measurement directions expose the distinction.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Show the optimal axes|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
A test needs many pairs, two settings per side, statistical uncertainties and unbiased pairing of the records. Check that the stations cannot communicate their settings during the measurements.

$$\widehat E=(N_{++}+N_{--}-N_{+-}-N_{-+})/N$$

+++ A closer look
The simulation samples the quantum formula to teach the analysis. Experimental evidence comes from actual measurements independently of the assumed distribution. Do not estimate E after selecting only trials on which the stations agree. That would select the sample using the very outcome under investigation. Decide how to match records and handle missed events before examining the signs.
+++

> [Lịch sử] John Bell proved his inequality in 1964; Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt gave the CHSH form in 1969. Freedman and Clauser made the first measurement with photon pairs in 1972. In 1982 Alain Aspect's group at Orsay measured S = 2.697 ± 0.015, very close to the quantum prediction, and added an experiment in which the axes were switched periodically while the photons were in flight. In 2015 three groups, at Delft, Vienna and NIST, closed the two main «loopholes» at once: the stations were far enough apart that they could not signal to each other in time, and the detectors were efficient enough that no trials had to be discarded. The Delft group used electron spins in diamond and measured S = 2.42 ± 0.20. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger.

> [Lưu ý] Photon experiments measure polarization, not spin. The correlation then goes as cos 2(a − b), so every angle is halved: the optimal axes are 22.5° apart instead of 45°.

bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A state of two spins with total spin angular momentum zero.
bai.moTa: Rotate two spin analyzers and match the outcomes of each pair to test the CHSH bound.
bai.yChinh: In a singlet of two particles of spin ½ each side sees random outcomes. Matching the records exposes correlations that can exceed the local hidden-variable bound when settings are independently chosen.
bai.giaiThich: The source in the middle sends pairs of particles to the two stations, Alice and Bob; the two particles of a pair share a colour. Each station is a Stern–Gerlach magnet that turns about the beam axis; the orange-red lamp signals +1, the blue lamp −1. The logbook at the back matches the two stations' results by emission number. All axes lie in one plane. In «four settings» mode each station chooses at random between a = 0° and a′ = 90°, between b and b′ = −b, and S is computed from the counts themselves. Distances and flight speed are shrunk and slowed.
bai.conSo.1: On identical axes every pair has opposite signs.
bai.conSo.2: Both local plus probabilities are always ½.
bai.hieuDung: Revealing the correlation requires comparing both records over an ordinary communication channel. One side cannot send a message by changing its angle and thereby altering the other side’s local distribution.

canh.tt-nguon: Each emission sends one particle to each station. The two particles of a pair share a colour; with the hidden-variable source the colour is the direction λ the pair carries.
canh.tt-may: Records the spin sign on the selected axis.
canh.tt-so-ghi: Each row is one emission: the axis and sign recorded at each station, matched by emission number. The last column is the product A·B.
canh.do-thi: Graph: correlation E versus the angle difference a − b. Gold: quantum singlet, −cos(a − b). Pink dashed: the model's local hidden-variable source, a zigzag line. Red dots: counted E, red bars their standard errors.
bai.conSo.3: |S| = 2√2 ≈ 2.83 is the largest value quantum mechanics allows (the Tsirelson bound); every local hidden-variable model is capped at 2.
